faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my North Charleston attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a North Charleston home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: A skunk is living under my Folly Beach deck. How is that handled?
faqs.a: A skunk under a deck wants two things: shelter and grubs, and Folly Beach yards near island's beach houses and marsh edge along the Folly River supply both. We set covered traps right at the den entrance to keep the animal calm, remove it under depredation rules, and then bury hardware cloth along the deck edge so the den cannot be re-dug. Skunks rank second only to raccoons in SC Department of Public Health rabies testing, which is why we do not recommend reaching, prodding, or trying to smoke one out.

faqs.q: Mole tunnels are tearing up my Folly Beach yard. Can you stop them?
faqs.a: Raised tunnels and soft ridges across a Folly Beach lawn are eastern mole work — the animal is hunting earthworms and grubs a few inches down and rarely comes above ground. We trap on the active travel tunnels, confirmed by pressing a section down and checking it the next day, rather than scattering repellents that only move the animal to the next yard. In sandy soil near island's beach houses and marsh edge along the Folly River, fresh tunnels can appear overnight after rain.

Structure decides the labor, since older housing near island's beach houses and marsh edge along the Folly River often hides several entries behind additions and repairs. Season decides the timing, especially when litters or bat pups mean part of the work waits a few weeks. You get the full picture from the inspection before committing to the plan.
